title: Question 7

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State and explain how Fig. 7.2 indicates that there is a systematic error in the readings of one of the meters.

markscheme_points.text: line has non-zero intercept/line does not pass through origin
charge is/should be proportional to potential (difference) or charge is/should be zero when p.d. is zero (therefore there is a systematic error)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what you expect for an uncharged capacitor - if the p.d. across it is truly zero, what must the stored charge be?
Hint 2: Imagine drawing a straight best-fit line through the points in Fig. 7.2 and extending it back - where does it meet the axes compared to where theory says it should meet?
parts.proper_answer: The best-fit straight line does not pass through the origin / has a non-zero intercept. Since $Q$ should be proportional to $V$ with $Q = 0$ when $V = 0$, this indicates a systematic (zero) error in one meter.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall What Theory Predicts**
For a capacitor, charge and p.d. are directly proportional: $$Q = CV$$ This is a straight line through the origin. When $V = 0$, there is no separation of charge, so $Q$ must be $0$.

Step 2: **Compare With Fig. 7.2**
The points in Fig. 7.2 lie on a good straight line, but that line if extended backwards would cut the $V$-axis at about $0.6\text{ V}$ instead of $0$, or equivalently cut the $Q$-axis below zero. It does not go through $(0,0)$. A shift of all readings by a fixed amount in one direction is the signature of a systematic error, for example a zero error on the voltmeter or charge meter.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Use Fig. 7.2 to determine the capacitance, in $\mu\text{F}$, of capacitor $C$.

markscheme_points.text: reasonable attempt at line of best fit
use of gradient of line of best fit clear

hints: Hint 1: Start from how $Q$ and $V$ are linked for a capacitor - if you write it in the form $y = mx$, what does the gradient $m$ represent?
Hint 2: Draw a best-fit straight line with even spread of points above and below, then pick two points on your line far apart to get $\Delta Q$ and $\Delta V$, not just the plotted dots.
Hint 3: Check your units carefully - $Q$ is in $\text{mC}$ on the graph, but capacitance in farads needs $Q$ in coulombs, then convert the final farad value to $\mu\text{F}$.
parts.proper_answer: Capacitance = gradient of $Q$-$V$ line, $C = \Delta Q / \Delta V \approx 2800\,\mu\text{F}$ (allow $\pm 200\,\mu\text{F}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Gradient Means Capacitance**
You know $$Q = CV$$ Compare with $y = mx$. Plotting $Q$ on the $y$-axis against $V$ on the $x$-axis gives a straight line of gradient $C$: $$C = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta V}$$ The systematic shift does not change the gradient, so you can still find the true $C$.

Step 2: **Draw Best-Fit Line and Choose a Large Triangle**
Draw a straight best-fit line through the points. Then read off two widely separated points on the line to reduce percentage uncertainty. For example: $$Q_1 \approx 0 \text{ at } V_1 \approx 0.6\text{ V}$$ $$Q_2 \approx 14.0\text{ mC at } V_2 \approx 5.6\text{ V}$$ So: $$\Delta Q \approx 14.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$$ $$\Delta V \approx 5.6 - 0.6 = 5.0\text{ V}$$

Step 3: **Calculate and Convert to Microfarads**
$$C = \frac{14.0 \times 10^{-3}}{5.0} \approx 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ F}$$ Since $1\,\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\text{ F}$: $$C \approx 2.8 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{6} = 2800\,\mu\text{F}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Use your answer in (b) to determine the additional energy stored in the capacitor $C$ when the potential difference across it is increased from $6.0\text{ V}$ to $9.0\text{ V}$.

markscheme_points.text: energy = ½ CV 2 or energy = ½ QV and C = Q / V

hints: Hint 1: Remember how the energy held in a capacitor depends on $C$ and $V$ - it is not simply proportional to $V$, so you cannot just use the voltage increase alone.
Hint 2: The word additional is important - you need the energy at 9.0 V minus the energy already stored at 6.0 V.
Hint 3: Convert your capacitance from (b) from $\mu\text{F}$ back to farads ($\times 10^{-6}$) before multiplying by $V^2$ to get joules.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the Stored Energy Formula**
Energy stored in a capacitor charged to p.d. $V$ is: $$E = \frac{1}{2}QV = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$$ You have $C$ from (b), so use the $CV^2$ version.

Step 2: **Set Up the Difference**
Additional energy is final minus initial: $$\Delta E = \frac{1}{2}C V_{2}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}C V_{1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}C(V_{2}^{2} - V_{1}^{2})$$ with $V_1 = 6.0\text{ V}$, $V_2 = 9.0\text{ V}$ and $C = 2800 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$.

Step 3: **Insert Numbers**
$$\Delta E = \frac{1}{2} \times 2800 \times 10^{-6} \times (9.0^2 - 6.0^2)$$ $$\Delta E = 1400 \times 10^{-6} \times (81 - 36)$$ $$\Delta E = 1400 \times 10^{-6} \times 45 = 6.3 \times 10^{-2}\text{ J}$$ This is the extra work done charging from 6.0 V to 9.0 V.
